47 KM/S
Why are galaxies not
flying apart into total
chaos right now?
According to the established
laws of physics,
they should be.
The story of how
we found out begins
with a simple question
about speed.
In our solar system,
distant planets drift lazily
while inner worlds race
around the Sun.
Mercury speeds along at
roughly forty-seven
kilometers per second,
while distant Neptune plods
along at less than six.
The farther out you
go, the slower the orbit.
Astronomers expected the
same rule in galaxies.
According to the established
laws of physics,
stars near the outer
rim of a galaxy
should move much slower
than stars near the
crowded center.
Then, beginning around
1970, the astronomer Vera
Rubin and her colleague
Kent Ford measured how
fast stars orbit in
the Andromeda galaxy,
and later in many
other spiral galaxies.
The outer stars were
not slowing down.
They were moving
astonishingly fast, and
their speeds stayed almost
flat all the way
to the edge of
the visible disk.
These stars were moving
so rapidly that the
visible gravity of the
galaxy could not possibly
hold them.
By all ordinary logic,
these swirling galaxies
should have torn themselves
apart and flung their
stars into the dark
void long ago.
Yet, they remain beautifully
intact.
Scientists suspect that
an immense, invisible halo
of mysterious mass surrounds
each galaxy, providing
the extra gravitational
glue needed to hold
everything together.
Because this substance
emits no light,
absorbs no light,
and reflects no light,
we simply call it dark matter.
Other evidence agrees.
Massive clusters of galaxies
stretch the light of
galaxies far behind them
into glowing arcs,
and the bending is
stronger than the visible
matter can explain.
The extra mass is
clearly there.
It simply does not shine.
Dark matter is not
made of protons,
neutrons, or electrons.
If a cloud of
it passed through your
living room right now,
you would not see
it, hear it, or feel it.
It interacts with our
world almost entirely
through gravity, yet its
invisible grip controls
the cosmos.
What could this mysterious
phantom matter really be?
Leading hypotheses suggest
undiscovered subatomic
particles, but no one
knows for sure.
Discover the full cosmic
mystery right now on
